title: The Mental Health Act 2025: what is and is not in force
blurb: Know which 2025 reforms are coming, which tiny parts are live, and why the 1983 rules still apply on the ward.
question: In October 2026 a patient detained under section 3 tells you she has read that the Mental Health Act 2025 lets her choose a 'nominated person' instead of a nearest relative, and that section 3 now lasts 3 months. How should you respond?

teach.h: Passed, but mostly not switched on
teach.body: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025. It amends the Mental Health Act 1983 rather than replacing it. Most of its reforms only take effect when the Secretary of State makes commencement regulations, and as at October 2026 almost all of them have not been commenced. In plain English: the new law exists on paper, but on the ward you still apply the 1983 Act as amended.

items.label: Royal Assent; final provisions in force
Restricted patient and youth transfer provisions in force
HRA extended to private MHA providers; CQC under-18 review duty
Main reforms phased in by regulations

teach.caption: Only one commencement regulation (SI 2026/385) had been made as at October 2026.

teach.h: The four coming principles (not yet in force)
teach.caption: These will replace the Code's five guiding principles in s118 once commenced.

head: Reform
Effect when commenced
rows: Removed from s3 detention (s2 still possible)
Serious harm test; likelihood of harm considered
Statutory plans for detained and CTO patients
NHS England and ICBs to help people make them
Opt-out for compulsory patients; access extended to informal in-patients

teach.body: Until a provision is commenced, it has no effect. So on every ward in England you apply the 1983 Act as amended and the 2015 Code of Practice: the nearest relative, 6-month s3, the three-month medication rule, 14-day s2 tribunal window and the current police station rules. When a patient or colleague asks about the 2025 Act, explain that it is law-in-waiting, and check for new commencement regulations rather than assuming.

You acknowledge her research and explain gently that the 2025 Act has passed but the nominated person and the 3-month s3 period have not yet been brought into force. Today her nearest relative is still decided by the s26 list, and her s3 lasts up to 6 months before renewal. You repeat her s132 rights, offer an IMHA to help her understand, and note that if her nearest relative is unsuitable, displacement through the county court is the current route.

teach.text: Royal Assent is not commencement. A provision only changes practice from the date set by regulations. Never apply the 2025 Act's nominated person, shorter durations, new criteria or police-station ban as current law until they are commenced.

items: Royal Assent 18 December 2025; most reforms need commencement regulations.
In force so far: technical provisions, some restricted-patient and youth transfer changes, HRA extension to private providers, CQC review duty.
Not in force: principles, nominated person, autism and LD changes, new criteria, shorter periods, care and treatment plans, police-station ban.
Practice now: the 1983 Act as amended and the 2015 Code.

summary: You can now explain that the Mental Health Act 2025 is mostly not yet in force, name the main coming reforms, and apply the current 1983 Act rules in practice. You know to check for commencement regulations before treating any reform as live.

A.q: On what date did the Mental Health Act 2025 receive Royal Assent?
A.why: The Mental Health Act 2025 (c. 33) received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025.

whyNot.1: 6 April 2026 is when ss51-52 were commenced by SI 2026/385.
whyNot.2: 18 February 2026 is when a small group of provisions came into force, two months after Assent.
whyNot.3: 1 April 2025 predates the Act's Royal Assent.

A.q: In October 2026, a detained patient asks who acts as her statutory relative under the Mental Health Act. What is accurate?
options: A nominated person she has chosen herself
A.why: The nominated person provisions of the 2025 Act are not in force, so the s26 nearest relative rules of the 1983 Act still apply.

whyNot.0: The nominated person is a 2025 Act reform that has not been commenced.
whyNot.2: An IMHA advocates but does not hold nearest relative powers.
whyNot.3: A care coordinator has no statutory relative role.

A.q: In October 2026, what is the maximum first period of detention under section 3?
A.why: The 2025 Act's reduction to 3 months is not in force; s20 of the 1983 Act still sets 6 months.

whyNot.0: Three months is a coming change that has not been commenced.
whyNot.2: Twelve-month periods apply to later renewals, not the first period.

B.q: Mr Ahmed, 34, is detained under section 136. No health-based place of safety can manage his imminently dangerous behaviour. In October 2026, can a police station be used?
options: No, the 2025 Act has removed police stations
Yes, for up to 72 hours with an inspector's consent
No, police stations are barred for adults
B.why: The 2025 Act provision removing police stations as places of safety is not in force. Under current law an adult may be taken there in the limited circumstances in the Places of Safety Regulations 2017.

whyNot.1: That 2025 Act reform has not been commenced.
whyNot.2: The limit is 24 hours plus up to 12, not 72 hours.
whyNot.3: The current bar applies to under-18s; adults may go in tightly limited cases.

B.q: A patient has been detained and medicated for 10 weeks. A colleague says a SOAD certificate is now needed 'because of the new Act'. What is the current rule?
options: A certificate is needed from 2 months
A certificate is needed from 6 weeks
A certificate is needed from 3 months
A certificate is needed from day 1
B.why: Section 58 of the 1983 Act still sets three months; the 2025 Act change to two months is not in force.

whyNot.0: Two months is a coming 2025 Act change, not current law.
whyNot.3: Medication can be given under s63 until the three-month point.

B.q: Lena, an autistic adult with no other mental disorder, meets the section 3 criteria. In October 2026, which is correct?
options: Section 3 is barred for autistic people
Section 3 can be used if its criteria are met
Detention must be under section 2 instead
A CTO must be used in place of hospital detention
B.why: Autism is a mental disorder under s1 of the 1983 Act, and the 2025 Act change removing autism from s3 detention is not in force.

whyNot.0: That bar is a coming reform, not current law.
whyNot.2: Restricting autism and LD to s2 is part of the uncommenced reforms.
whyNot.3: A CTO requires prior s3 detention and is not a substitute.

C.q: Josh was detained under section 2 on Monday. He has read online that he has 21 days to apply to the tribunal. In October 2026, what should his nurse tell him?
C.why: Section 66(2)(a) of the 1983 Act still gives a s2 patient 14 days; the 2025 Act change to 21 days is not in force.

whyNot.0: Twenty-one days is a coming change that has not been commenced.
whyNot.1: 28 days is the length of s2, not the application window.
whyNot.3: Six months is the s3 window.

C.q: Which principles must guide decisions under the Mental Health Act in October 2026?
options: The four statutory principles in the 2025 Act
The five guiding principles in the 2015 Code
The six principles of the Care Act
C.why: The 2025 Act principles are not in force, so the 2015 Code's five guiding principles still apply.

whyNot.0: The four statutory principles await commencement.
whyNot.1: The MCA principles govern capacity decisions under that Act.
whyNot.3: Care Act principles relate to adult social care, not MHA decisions.

C.q: Which of these is a reform of the Mental Health Act 2025 that is NOT yet in force?
C.why: Statutory care and treatment plans (new s130ZA) are a 2025 Act reform awaiting commencement.

whyNot.0: The under-18 police station bar has been in force since December 2017.
whyNot.2: The 24-hour limit has applied since December 2017.
whyNot.3: Written and oral s132 information is a long-standing 1983 Act duty.

reteach.title: Paper law and ward law
reteach.question: How do you decide whether a reform applies today?

blocks.body: An Act can pass Parliament and still change nothing until a commencement date arrives. The 2025 Act gave the Secretary of State power to commence most of it by regulations at different times. Only a handful of technical and specialist provisions are live. Everything a ward nurse uses daily, from holding powers to nearest relatives, is still the 1983 Act as amended.

steps.label: Commencement regs
steps.sub: Secretary of State sets the date

blocks.text: If a source says 'the new Act says', check the commencement position before you change practice.

explain.body: Section 56 of the 2025 Act brought a few provisions in on Royal Assent and some two months later; everything else waits for regulations made by the Secretary of State, which can set different days for different purposes.

test.q: How are most provisions of the Mental Health Act 2025 brought into force?
options: By a resolution of both Houses of Parliament
On a date fixed in the Act, 12 months after Assent
By publication of a revised Code of Practice
By regulations made by the Secretary of State
test.why: Section 56(3): except for listed provisions, the Act comes into force on days appointed by the Secretary of State by regulations.

whyNot.0: Parliament passed the Act; commencement is by ministerial regulations, not a further resolution.
whyNot.1: Section 56 fixes no 12-month date; it fixes Assent and two months for a few provisions.
whyNot.2: A Code is guidance; it does not commence legislation.

explain.body: Technical provisions (Assent); some restricted patient, tribunal and youth transfer changes (18 Feb 2026); s51 extending the Human Rights Act to private providers of MHA care and s52 CQC under-18 review duty (6 Apr 2026).

test.q: Which document commenced sections 51 and 52 of the Mental Health Act 2025?
test.why: The Mental Health Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/385, brought ss51 and 52 into force on 6 April 2026.

whyNot.2: The 2017 regulations govern police stations as places of safety.
whyNot.3: The 2017 Act changed place-of-safety time limits years earlier.

explain.body: Four statutory principles; nominated person replacing the nearest relative; autism and learning disability removed from s3; new detention criteria; shorter s3 and s58 periods; longer s2 tribunal window; care and treatment plans; advance choice documents; police stations removed as places of safety.

test.q: Which is one of the four principles set out in the Mental Health Act 2025 (not yet in force)?
test.why: The 2025 Act principles are choice and autonomy, least restriction, therapeutic benefit, and the person as an individual.

whyNot.0: Efficiency and equity is one of the current Code's five principles.
whyNot.1: Purpose and effectiveness is a current Code principle.
whyNot.3: Presumption of capacity is an MCA principle.

explain.body: Apply the 1983 Act as amended and the 2015 Code. When asked about reforms, explain they are coming, and check for any new commencement regulations.

test.q: A colleague wants to stop consulting a patient's nearest relative 'because the 2025 Act abolished them'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as the Act has now received Royal Assent
Agree, if the patient prefers it
Explain that the change is not yet in force
test.why: The nominated person provisions have not been commenced, so the nearest relative's statutory role continues.

whyNot.0: Royal Assent alone does not bring the provisions into force.
whyNot.1: The patient cannot choose to replace the NR under current law; displacement is by the county court.
whyNot.2: An IMHA has no power to decide this.
